text: Now it only remains to speak about ecclesiastical principalities. The only difficulties with these states happen before you take them. You can acquire them through ability or fortune, but you can keep them without either. They are sustained by the ancient laws of religion. These religious institutions are so powerful that they keep a prince in power regardless of how he behaves or lives. These are the only princes who have states but do not defend them, and who have subjects but do not rule them. Even though their states are unguarded, they are never taken away. Even though their subjects are not governed, they do not care, and they have neither the desire nor the ability to overthrow their rulers. Therefore, these are the only secure and happy principalities in the world. But since they are upheld by higher powers that the human mind cannot comprehend, I will not speak about them anymore. Since they are exalted and maintained by God, only a presumptuous and rash man would dare to discuss them.

However, someone might ask me how the Church has achieved such immense worldly power. Before the time of Pope Alexander the Sixth, the major Italian powers cared very little about the temporal power of the Church. Even the smallest barons and lords completely dismissed it. Yet today, a king of France trembles before it. The Church has been able to drive him out of Italy and completely ruin the Venetians. Even though the reasons for this rise to power might be obvious, it is still worth recalling exactly how it happened.

Before King Charles the Eighth of France invaded Italy in 1494, the country was ruled by the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These rulers had two main anxieties. First, they wanted to ensure that no foreign army entered Italy. Second, they wanted to prevent any one of them from expanding their territory. The two powers they worried about the most were the Pope and the Venetians. To hold back the Venetians, all the other powers had to unite, just as they did to defend Ferrara. To keep the Pope in check, they used the barons of Rome. These barons were divided into two warring factions, the Orsini and the Colonna. They always had an excuse for causing trouble. Standing armed right under the Pope's nose, they kept the pontificate weak and powerless. Occasionally, a courageous pope like Sixtus the Fourth would come along, but neither his fortune nor his wisdom could free him from these problems. The short lifespan of a pope was the main cause of this weakness. On average, a pope only lived for about ten years in office, and it was extremely difficult for him to crush even one of these factions. If one pope almost destroyed the Colonna, the next pope would rise up as an enemy of the Orsini and bring the Colonna back to power, yet he would never have enough time to completely destroy the Orsini. This constant infighting was exactly why the worldly power of the Pope was respected so little in Italy.

Then Pope Alexander the Sixth came into power. Out of all the pontiffs who have ever lived, he was the one who showed exactly how a pope could dominate using both money and armed force. Using Duke Valentino as his instrument, and taking advantage of the French invasion, he accomplished everything I discussed earlier regarding the actions of the duke. Even though Alexander's true intention was to empower his son the duke, rather than the Church itself, his actions ultimately contributed to the greatness of the Church. After Alexander died and the duke was ruined, the Church inherited everything they had built.

Pope Julius the Second came next, and he inherited a very strong Church. It controlled all of the Romagna, the Roman barons were powerless, and Alexander's harsh punishments had wiped out the warring factions. Julius also found new ways to accumulate wealth that had never been practiced before Alexander's time. Julius not only continued these practices, but he improved upon them. He set out to conquer Bologna, destroy the Venetians, and drive the French entirely out of Italy. All of these aggressive campaigns were highly successful. He deserves even more credit because he did everything to strengthen the Church, rather than to enrich any private individual. He also kept the Orsini and Colonna factions strictly within the bounds he found them. Although some of them wanted to stir up trouble, Julius held them down using two firm tactics. First, he terrified them with the immense power of the Church. Second, he refused to let them appoint their own cardinals. The cardinals were the root cause of all the unrest between them. Whenever these factions have their own cardinals, they never stay quiet for long. Cardinals foster the factions both inside and outside of Rome, and the barons are forced to defend them. In this way, the ambitions of religious prelates always cause disorders and riots among the barons. Thanks to these ruthless and calculating strategies, His Holiness Pope Leo the Tenth inherited a supremely powerful pontificate. Since his predecessors made the Church great through force of arms, we can only hope that Leo will make it even greater and more deeply respected through his goodness and his infinite other virtues.
